Roscelin
rŏs´e-lĭn
n. (Roscelin of Compiègne, c. 1050–c. 1125, the first great nominalist, whose application of nominalism to the Trinity was condemned as tritheism at Soissons in 1092)
Old French Roscelin, a Germanic diminutive; Latinized Roscelinus, of Compiègne.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Roscelin taught that universals are names only — that humanity is a word covering individual men and has no existence of its own. Applied to logic the thesis is defensible and became one of the two great medieval positions. Applied to the Godhead it was ruinous, and Roscelin applied it. If only individuals exist, and the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three, then the divine substance they are said to share is a mere name, and there are three Gods. He seems to have pressed this as a question rather than a dogma, but the conclusion was plain and the Council of Soissons condemned it in 1092; Anselm of Canterbury wrote his treatise on the incarnation of the Word against him. The answer is the Shema itself: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4), with 1Jn 5:7, “these three are one,” and Isa 45:5, “I am the LORD, and there is none else.” Roscelin is also remembered as the first teacher of Peter Abelard, who took his master's logic, avoided his heresy, and fell into another.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines nominalism by way of the nominalists, a sect of school philosophers who maintained that universals are mere names or words.

expand to see more

NOM'INALIST, n. One of a sect of school philosophers, the followers of Occam or Ockham, who maintained that universals have no real existence, but are mere names or words.

NOM'INAL, a. Titular; existing in name only; as a nominal distinction.

REALIST, n. One who maintains that universals have a real existence.

Key Scripture

Deu 6:4 — "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:"

1Jn 5:7 — "For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one."

Joh 14:9 — "Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?"

Isa 45:5 — "I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:"

Modern Corruption

Roscelin proves that a theory of language is never only that, and that a philosophy carried unexamined into theology will decide a doctrine before anyone notices.

expand to see more

The error was not that Roscelin reasoned badly within his system but that he let the system legislate for the Godhead. Nominalism answers a question about words; the Trinity is revealed, and the revelation includes both that God is one and that the Father, Son and Spirit are each that one God. When a philosophical commitment cannot carry both, the commitment yields. This is the permanent discipline for every theological use of a borrowed framework, and it applies as much to the modern borrowings — from psychology, sociology, process metaphysics — as to eleventh-century logic. “The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4) is not negotiable with a theory of universals.

The second corruption is the opposite excess the realists courted, and into which some Augustinians fell: making the divine essence a fourth thing in which the Persons participate, which is a quaternity. Scripture gives neither three Gods nor an essence behind the Persons. It gives one God subsisting in three Persons, each wholly God, distinguished by eternal relations and not by parts. Divine simplicity in the Reformed scholastic sense is the guard on both sides, and the Lord's own word to Philip settles the unity of operation and being: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (Joh 14:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew echad (H259), one; Greek heis (G1520), one; ousia, substance or essence (the term at issue).

expand to see more

Hebrew echad (H259) — one, a unity; Deuteronomy 6:4.

Greek heis (G1520) — one; 1 John 5:7.

Hebrew zulah (H2108) — besides, except; Isaiah 45:5.

Greek horao (G3708) — to see, to perceive; John 14:9.

Greek homoousios — of one substance, the word nominalism could not carry.

Usage

"“The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4) — the word his logic could not hold."

"“and these three are one” (1Jn 5:7) — against tritheism."

"“he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (Joh 14:9) — one being, not three Gods."
